content: To ensure sustainability, the strategic information system for the health sector's response to HIV must be aligned with the broader health information system (HIS) as part of an integrated architecture. National HIS standards and tools are available to support the development of appropriate HIS and digital health policies, guidelines, strategic plans, and roadmaps, including system interoperability. Routine programmatic data collection only captures information on individuals who actively seek health services at facilities or through community outreach. To gain a comprehensive understanding that includes individuals not reached by services, routine data should be supplemented with data from population-based surveys (e.g., Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), PHIA household surveys, and bio-behavioral surveys among key populations), models (e.g., Spectrum AIDS Impact Module (AIM)), and special studies. These additional data sources help triangulate and validate assessments of program performance, including impact. Many health services are delivered in community settings to improve access for individuals who may prefer these settings over traditional health facilities. These outreach activities may be associated with health facilities or delivered through community-led organizations. Data systems must be capable of capturing and integrating data on community-based service delivery, whether provided via mobile or satellite clinics or by peer or outreach workers. Enabling bidirectional data flow between community-delivered services and health facilities in a standardized manner will facilitate program monitoring and data use for both types of services. With differentiated care, HIV prevention, testing, and treatment are increasingly provided at the community level, with links to facility services and data systems. Community engagement of people living with and affected by HIV, through community-led monitoring, is critical to improving the quality of HIV services. Community engagement fosters an environment where stakeholders collaborate to address health-related issues, promote well-being, and achieve positive health outcomes. The 2021 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring incorporated guidance on community-led monitoring to enhance the quality of HIV service delivery for people living with HIV. Structured input from community-led monitoring is an essential component of a national HIV health information system. Community-led monitoring operates independently of routine health care service delivery and clinical data-based information systems, serving as an accountability mechanism that empowers communities to monitor access to and quality of health services and drive change. It positions community groups as key actors in decision-making processes to improve and shape services. The 2022 Consolidated Guidelines on person-centered HIV strategic information aim to provide a unified resource for recommended data elements, indicators, and guidance on data systems and use across the spectrum of health sector HIV services. These guidelines consolidate clinical recommendations and introduce a minimum dataset for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and related infections, such as STIs, viral hepatitis, and cervical cancer. This approach supports the evolution of HIV guidelines toward comprehensive, holistic, and SMART (Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable) guideline products. The guidelines emphasize the importance of individual-level data in HIV prevention services, monitoring individuals at substantial risk of HIV, and addressing issues such as early diagnosis, late ART initiation, re-engagement in care, advanced HIV disease, and differentiated service delivery. They also highlight the integration of individual-level data on viral hepatitis, STIs, TB, and cervical cancer to strengthen links to person-centered health services over the life course of individuals at elevated risk of HIV acquisition and those living with HIV. Routine programmatic data play a critical role in measuring and monitoring HIV incidence in programs, strengthening the focus on impact. The guidelines also address the governance of digital health data during the transition from paper-based to digital systems, emphasizing interoperability, unique identifiers, data security, privacy, confidentiality, and data access. Digital adaptation kits (DAKs) are included in the guidelines to support the design of person-centered digital tracking and decision-support systems. These systems combine an individual's health information with clinical protocols to assist health workers in making diagnosis and treatment decisions aligned with WHO recommendations. They also link to reporting and management tools to support accountability. The overarching goal of these guidelines is to support countries in generating responsive, person-centered data from routine national health information management systems. By keeping the individual at the center and understanding how people access services, health decision-making and outcomes can be improved. The guidelines aim to strengthen data analysis and use at each stage of the HIV service cascade, emphasizing person-centered prevention, testing, and treatment, integration of related infections, routine surveillance data for impact measurement, and the development and governance of digital health data systems. Countries are at different stages of digital health maturity and can adopt interventions, datasets, and indicators appropriate to their context. Interoperability among services and programs during the expansion of national HIS can facilitate data exchange and use for action, supporting progress toward comprehensive person-centered data systems.
